title: 2 Kings 10:1–17
context: Jehu writes to the leaders in Samaria, challenging them to set one of Ahab’s seventy sons on the throne and fight. Afraid, they submit, and at his second letter they kill the seventy sons and send their heads to Jezreel. Jehu presents this to the people as the LORD fulfilling His word through Elijah, then kills the rest of Ahab’s household and officials in Jezreel. On the road he kills forty-two relatives of Ahaziah of Judah. He meets Jehonadab son of Rechab, takes him into his chariot to see his zeal for the LORD, and in Samaria destroys all who remained of Ahab’s house, which the narrator ties to the LORD’s word to Elijah.

verses.text: Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of Jezreel, even the elders, and to those who brought up Ahab’s sons, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab has seventy sons in Samaria, and Jehu writes to the leaders and guardians there. Arminian readers note that Jehu uses letters to pressure the leaders of the capital, testing their loyalty before acting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the number of sons as showing the size of the dynasty under judgment. Both traditions read the verse as moving the story from Jezreel to Samaria, where Ahab’s house still has its strongest support.

verses.text: “Now as soon as this letter comes to you, since your master’s sons are with you, and you have chariots and horses, a fortified city also, and armor,
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu notes that the leaders have their master’s sons, chariots, horses, a fortified city, and weapons. Arminian readers see a calculated challenge, listing the resources they would need to resist him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the letter as exposing the leaders’ fear, since they know they cannot stand against Jehu. Shared ground: the verse sets up a test of loyalty, with Jehu inviting them to fight if they dare.

verses.text: select the best and fittest of your master’s sons, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu tells them to choose the best of Ahab’s sons, set him on the throne, and fight. Arminian readers note that the challenge forces the leaders to decide openly where they stand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the challenge as a means of drawing out the leaders’ submission. Both traditions read the verse as a strategic move by Jehu, reported as part of the political struggle that follows.

verses.text: But they were exceedingly afraid, and said, “Behold, the two kings didn’t stand before him! How then shall we stand?”
verses.arminianNotes: The leaders are greatly afraid, reasoning that if two kings could not stand, neither can they. Arminian readers see fear shaping their response, as they weigh their own survival above loyalty to Ahab’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fear as part of God’s providence in bringing the dynasty to its end. Shared ground: the verse shows the leaders’ recognition that resistance is hopeless after the deaths of Joram and Ahaziah.

verses.text: He who was over the household, and he who was over the city, the elders also, and those who raised the children, sent to Jehu, saying, “We are your servants, and will do all that you ask us. We will not make any man king. You do that which is good in your eyes.”
verses.arminianNotes: The officials and guardians submit to Jehu, promising to do whatever he asks. Arminian readers note that they choose submission freely, out of fear, and will bear responsibility for what they do next.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the leaders giving up any claim to independent action. Both traditions read the verse as a political surrender that leaves Ahab’s sons without protection from those charged to care for them.

verses.text: Then he wrote a letter the second time to them, saying, “If you are on my side, and if you will listen to my voice, take the heads of the men who are your master’s sons, and come to me to Jezreel by tomorrow this time.” Now the king’s sons, being seventy persons, were with the great men of the city, who brought them up.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu’s second letter demands the heads of Ahab’s sons by the next day. Arminian readers state the demand plainly as the text gives it, noting that Jehu makes the leaders of Samaria agents of the killing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the demand as part of the judgment announced on Ahab’s house, while recognizing that the text records rather than commends Jehu’s methods. Shared ground: both traditions report the verse soberly.

verses.text: When the letter came to them, they took the king’s sons and killed them, even seventy people, and put their heads in baskets, and sent them to him to Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: The leaders kill the seventy sons and send their heads to Jezreel. Arminian readers note that those who raised the sons carry out the killing, showing how fear can override every other loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the event within the judgment on Ahab’s house. Both traditions report the verse as the text gives it, without elaboration, and neither treats it as a model for anyone’s conduct.

verses.text: A messenger came and told him, “They have brought the heads of the king’s sons.” He said, “Lay them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until the morning.”
verses.arminianNotes: The heads are placed in two heaps at the city gate until morning. Arminian readers note that the display was a public act meant to show that the old dynasty had ended and to deter resistance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the public setting as part of Jehu’s effort to show the people what had happened. Shared ground: the verse is reported briefly, and both traditions decline to dwell on it beyond what the text says.

verses.text: In the morning, he went out and stood, and said to all the people, “You are righteous. Behold, I conspired against my master and killed him, but who killed all these?
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu tells the people they are righteous and asks who killed all these, since he killed only his master. Arminian readers see a shrewd political speech that spreads responsibility to the leaders of Samaria.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jehu’s words serve his purposes, and the narrator does not endorse his reasoning. Both traditions read the speech as an attempt to win the people’s support by sharing the guilt of the killings.

verses.text: Know now that nothing will fall to the earth of the LORD’s word, which the LORD spoke concerning Ahab’s house. For the LORD has done that which he spoke by his servant Elijah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu declares that none of the LORD’s word against Ahab’s house will fall to the ground. Arminian readers note that Jehu appeals to the prophetic word to justify what has happened, as the narrator also does in 10:17.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as affirming that God’s word through Elijah will be fulfilled completely. Shared ground: both traditions agree that the narrator presents these events as fulfilling Elijah’s prophecy (1 Kings 21:21–24).

verses.text: So Jehu struck all that remained of Ahab’s house in Jezreel, with all his great men, his familiar friends, and his priests, until he left him no one remaining.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu kills all that remained of Ahab’s house in Jezreel, including officials, friends, and priests. Arminian readers note that the killings extend beyond the royal family to its supporters, a reach the text records without comment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as completing the judgment in Jezreel. Both traditions report the verse soberly, and many note that Hosea 1:4 seems to contain a later word about the bloodshed at Jezreel, read in different ways.

verses.text: He arose and departed, and went to Samaria. As he was at the shearing house of the shepherds on the way,
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu sets out for Samaria and comes to the shearing house of the shepherds on the way. Arminian readers note that the location is uncertain, and that the narrative moves quickly from one scene of judgment to another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the journey as the next stage of Jehu’s campaign against Ahab’s house. Shared ground: the place name, often rendered Beth Eked, cannot be identified with confidence, and the verse simply sets the scene.

verses.text: Jehu met with the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah, and said, “Who are you?” They answered, “We are the brothers of Ahaziah. We are going down to greet the children of the king and the children of the queen.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu meets the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah, who are going to greet the royal family. Arminian readers note that they are unaware of what has happened, traveling to visit relatives who are already dead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their connection to Ahab’s house through Ahaziah’s mother as the reason they are caught in the purge. Both traditions read the verse as showing how far the ties between Judah and Ahab’s house had reached.

verses.text: He said, “Take them alive!” They took them alive, and killed them at the pit of the shearing house, even forty-two men. He didn’t leave any of them.
verses.arminianNotes: Forty-two kinsmen of Ahaziah are seized at the pit of the shearing house and put to death. Arminian readers observe that no prophetic word is cited for this killing, and the narrator offers no approval of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the text does not directly connect this killing to the prophetic word, unlike 10:10 and 10:17. Shared ground: both traditions report the verse soberly and do not treat it as a model.

verses.text: When he had departed from there, he met Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him. He greeted him, and said to him, “Is your heart right, as my heart is with your heart?” Jehonadab answered, “It is.” “If it is, give me your hand.” He gave him his hand; and he took him up to him into the chariot.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu meets Jehonadab son of Rechab and takes him into his chariot. Arminian readers note that Jehonadab appears later as the ancestor of the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35, by reference), though the link is not spelled out here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jehu seeking the support of a respected figure loyal to the LORD. Both traditions acknowledge that little is known about Jehonadab beyond these verses and Jeremiah 35, and avoid speculating about his motives.

verses.text: He said, “Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD.” So they made him ride in his chariot.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu tells Jehonadab to come and see his zeal for the LORD. Arminian readers note the self-description, which the narrator later qualifies by noting that Jehu did not walk in the LORD’s law with all his heart (10:31).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Jehu’s words a zeal that is real in some ways but mixed with self-interest. Shared ground: both traditions read his claim to zeal alongside the narrator’s later verdict, rather than taking it at face value.

verses.text: When he came to Samaria, he struck all who remained to Ahab in Samaria, until he had destroyed them, according to the LORD’s word which he spoke to Elijah.
verses.arminianNotes: In Samaria Jehu destroys all who remained of Ahab’s house, according to the LORD’s word to Elijah. Arminian readers note that the narrator here explicitly links the killings to the prophetic word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as confirming that God’s announced judgment on Ahab’s house reached its end. Both traditions agree that the text presents this as fulfillment of Elijah’s word, while also recording Jehu’s later failings.
